gaps.concept: ADH is synthesized in hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, transported with neurophysin II, and released from the neuroectoderm-derived posterior pituitary.
gaps.why_tested: A lesion interrupts the pituitary stalk; the question asks where ADH is made or which tissue releases it.

gaps.concept: V2 receptors signal through Gs, cAMP, and PKA; V1 receptors signal through Gq, phospholipase C, IP3, and calcium.
gaps.why_tested: A receptor or second-messenger question asks how ADH inserts aquaporin-2 or contracts vascular smooth muscle.

gaps.concept: Gestational DI results from placental vasopressinase degrading maternal ADH; desmopressin resists this enzyme.
gaps.why_tested: A pregnant patient develops new polyuria and dilute urine that responds to desmopressin.

gaps.concept: Inherited nephrogenic DI is usually X-linked AVPR2 loss of function; AQP2 defects are usually autosomal recessive.
gaps.why_tested: A boy with lifelong polyuria has affected maternal male relatives or a pedigree suggesting recessive inheritance.

gaps.concept: Autosomal dominant AVP–neurophysin II mutations cause familial central DI.
gaps.why_tested: Multiple generations develop childhood-onset polyuria that responds to desmopressin.

gaps.concept: Central DI often lacks the normal posterior pituitary T1 MRI bright spot, reflecting depleted ADH-containing granules.
gaps.why_tested: A pituitary MRI accompanies persistent polyuria after hypothalamic or stalk injury.

gaps.concept: Pituitary stalk injury can cause DI, then transient SIADH from ADH release, then permanent DI after stores are depleted.
gaps.why_tested: Urine output and serum sodium change in three phases after pituitary surgery or head trauma.

gaps.concept: Primary polydipsia usually has low or low-normal serum sodium and osmolality, unlike DI with uncompensated free-water loss.
gaps.why_tested: Two patients have dilute polyuria; baseline blood tests help distinguish excess intake from impaired water conservation.

gaps.concept: Diabetes mellitus causes osmotic polyuria with glucosuria and elevated urine osmolality, unlike the hypotonic polyuria of DI.
gaps.why_tested: A patient presents with thirst and frequent urination; urinalysis distinguishes solute diuresis from DI.

gaps.concept: Intact thirst and water access can keep serum sodium normal in DI; impaired thirst or restricted access permits severe hypernatremia.
gaps.why_tested: A patient has marked dilute polyuria but normal sodium, or develops hypernatremia after losing access to water.

gaps.concept: Thiazides reduce nephrogenic DI polyuria by causing mild volume contraction and increased proximal sodium and water reabsorption.
gaps.why_tested: A question asks why a diuretic paradoxically lowers urine volume in nephrogenic DI.

gaps.concept: Amiloride blocks ENaC-mediated lithium entry into collecting-duct principal cells, limiting lithium-induced nephrogenic DI.
gaps.why_tested: A lithium-treated patient develops polyuria; the question asks why amiloride helps.

gaps.concept: Desmopressin can cause water retention, dilutional hyponatremia, and seizures when water intake is excessive.
gaps.why_tested: A patient treated for central DI develops headache, confusion, or seizures with low serum sodium.

gaps.concept: SIADH produces hypotonic hyponatremia; hyperglycemic hyponatremia has increased effective osmolality, while lipid-related pseudohyponatremia has normal measured osmolality.
gaps.why_tested: A low sodium result must be classified using glucose and measured serum osmolality.

gaps.concept: In SIADH, mild volume expansion promotes natriuresis, leaving patients clinically euvolemic without peripheral edema.
gaps.why_tested: A question asks why urine sodium is high despite water retention and no visible edema.

gaps.concept: SIADH commonly lowers serum uric acid and BUN through water retention and increased urate excretion.
gaps.why_tested: Additional laboratory values help identify SIADH in a patient with hypotonic hyponatremia.

gaps.concept: Cerebral salt wasting causes hypovolemic hyponatremia with high urine sodium after intracranial disease; SIADH is clinically euvolemic.
gaps.why_tested: A patient develops hyponatremia after brain injury; orthostasis or other volume findings distinguish the diagnoses.

gaps.concept: Secondary adrenal insufficiency and severe hypothyroidism can mimic SIADH; normal cortisol and thyroid function support SIADH.
gaps.why_tested: A patient has euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia and concentrated urine despite no obvious SIADH trigger.

gaps.concept: MDMA, chlorpropamide, and vincristine can cause SIADH; MDMA also increases thirst.
gaps.why_tested: A drug exposure precedes acute symptomatic hyponatremia with concentrated urine.

gaps.concept: Tolvaptan selectively blocks V2 receptors; conivaptan blocks V1a and V2 receptors, producing electrolyte-free water excretion.
gaps.why_tested: A pharmacology question asks how a vaptan raises serum sodium in SIADH.

gaps.concept: Langerhans cell histiocytosis can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and cause central DI, often with lytic skull lesions.
gaps.why_tested: A child has polyuria, polydipsia, and characteristic bone lesions.

gaps.concept: Wolfram syndrome from WFS1 defects combines central DI, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and deafness.
gaps.why_tested: A young patient has polyuria alongside progressive vision and hearing loss.
